links.label: the questions it inherited
links.reason: The Presocratics' questions and answers were the foundation on which philosophy as Plato and Aristotle defined it was built.

links.label: teacher, then target
links.reason: Aristotle studied in Plato's Academy before founding the Lyceum. Then: Aristotle criticised Plato's theory of Forms (it cannot explain change) and opposed Platonic dualism of soul and body.

links.label: materialism it rejected
links.reason: Aristotle saw the Presocratics as his predecessors but judged them unsuccessful, and rejected their materialist accounts of living things.

links.label: the atoms it borrowed
links.reason: Epicurus inherited his atomist physics from the earlier atomists, above all Democritus, and studied under a Democritean.

links.label: Forms it threw out
links.reason: Epicurus' materialism dispensed with Plato's transcendent Forms and denied that the soul survives death.

links.label: Socrates as model
links.reason: Zeno read Socratic dialogues and was influenced by Plato's Academy; Stoic psychology returns to Socrates' intellectualism.

links.label: the divided soul rejected
links.reason: Stoic psychology rejects the Platonic-Aristotelian idea of non-rational parts of the mature soul.

links.label: Socratic questioning
links.reason: Socrates' commitment to examination as the way to find out inspired the skepticism of the Hellenistic Academy.

links.label: certainty it attacked
links.reason: Academic skeptics Arcesilaus and Carneades attacked the Stoic criterion of truth and Stoic epistemology.

links.label: truth test it doubted
links.reason: The Academics questioned the Epicurean claim to a criterion of truth and defended skeptical action against Epicurean critics.

links.label: Plato as master
links.reason: The Neoplatonists called themselves Platonists and held Plato's views above all others; Plotinus took Plato as having laid the fundamentals.

links.label: texts it worked from
links.reason: Plotinus used passages of Aristotle's Metaphysics as starting points, and his sessions read commentaries on Plato and Aristotle.

links.label: materialism it refused
links.reason: Neoplatonists absorbed almost the whole Greek tradition except Epicureanism, which they rejected outright.

links.label: Platonism for faith
links.reason: At Milan Augustine met Neoplatonically inclined Christians who showed him a philosophically informed Christianity; through him and the Greek Fathers, Neoplatonism shaped Christian theology.

links.label: Stoic ethics taken up
links.reason: Christian writers took up some elements of Stoicism.

links.label: knowledge defended
links.reason: In Contra Academicos Augustine defended knowledge against the Academic skeptics.

sources.section: 5.1 Augustine: Re-Conceiving Skepticism in a Theological Framework

links.label: the rediscovered Aristotle
links.reason: Thirteenth-century university philosophers were enthused by newly available Aristotle; Aquinas worked to write commentaries on all of Aristotle's principal works.

sources.section: 1.2 The Platonic Schools of Late Antiquity

links.label: the Platonist frame
links.reason: Medieval Aristotelianism was transmitted in a Platonist context; via Augustine and Pseudo-Dionysius, Neoplatonism shaped Aquinas and Scotus.

sources.section: 1.2 The Platonic Schools of Late Antiquity

links.label: Augustine as inspiration
links.reason: Augustine's works were read widely in the Middle Ages and gave philosophers a source and inspiration.

sources.section: 2.2 The Rule and Two Exceptions: Latin Philosophy, 800–1100

links.label: school logic it mocked
links.reason: Petrarch set out what became the standard critique of scholastic philosophy, and fifteenth- and early sixteenth-century humanists condemned university education and scholastic logic.

links.label: Plato and Plotinus revived
links.reason: Ficino's translations of Plato and Plotinus led a dramatic Renaissance revival of Neoplatonism.

links.label: Neo-Stoic revival
links.reason: Renaissance thinkers renewed the study of Stoicism; SEP calls Justus Lipsius the most important figure of the Neo-Stoic movement.

sources.section: 5.3 On Renaissance and Early Modern Philosophy

links.label: Epicurus rediscovered
links.reason: The Renaissance's renewed study of Epicureanism (with other Hellenistic schools) loosened Aristotle's hold.

links.label: Sextus rediscovered
links.reason: Renaissance skepticism was inspired by the revival of ancient Greek skepticism, notably the rediscovery of Sextus Empiricus (1562).

sources.section: 5.1 Augustine: Re-Conceiving Skepticism in a Theological Framework

links.label: scholastic assumptions attacked
links.reason: Descartes attacked the assumptions of the scholastic Aristotelians that stood in the way of the new science.

links.label: no innate ideas
links.reason: Empiricists reject innate knowledge; Locke spends the whole first book of his Essay arguing against it.

links.label: pillar, then limits
links.reason: Descartes' rationalist system, with its method of doubt, is one of the pillars of Enlightenment thought. Then: Kant's early work was enmeshed in Leibniz-Wolff rationalism, until Hume shook his faith in its assumption that metaphysical knowledge is possible.

sources.section: b. Dogmatic Slumber, Synthetic A Priori Knowledge, and the Copernican Shift

links.label: Locke, then answering Hume
links.reason: The rise of empiricism is characteristic of the period; Locke's Essay is a foundational Enlightenment text. Then: Hume's skepticism woke Kant from his 'dogmatic slumber'; the critical philosophy was designed as an answer to Hume.

sources.section: b. Dogmatic Slumber, Synthetic A Priori Knowledge, and the Copernican Shift

links.label: skeptical tools against dogma
links.reason: Enlightenment thinkers used skeptical tropes drawn from the ancient skeptics to attack traditional dogmas.

links.label: Kant radicalised
links.reason: Fichte, Schelling and Hegel radicalised Kant's transcendental idealism into absolute idealism.

links.label: Hume's idea of utility
links.reason: Hume is an early precursor; Bentham found virtue equated with utility in Hume's Treatise and borrowed the term from him.

links.label: Helvétius and Beccaria
links.reason: Bentham found the utility principle in the writings of Hume, Helvétius and Beccaria; SEP places Helvétius in the radical French Enlightenment.

sources.section: 1.4 Science of Man and Subjectivism in the Enlightenment

links.label: Hegel turned upside down
links.reason: Marx took over Hegel's teleological account of history and 'inverted' it into a materialist theory, appropriating many Hegelian ideas.

links.label: Hegel's system rejected
links.reason: Kierkegaard's attack on detached theory was aimed mainly at Hegel's system; Schelling's critique of Hegel reached him too.

links.label: the method it used
links.reason: Heidegger took up his teacher Husserl's phenomenological maxim 'to the things themselves'; Husserl is named among the movement's groundwork.

links.label: experience, made radical
links.reason: James presented pragmatism as the empiricist attitude in a more radical form.

links.label: Cartesian certainty rejected
links.reason: The pragmatists set out to overcome Cartesianism, rejecting Descartes' individualist search for certainty.

links.label: Kant's thing-in-itself rejected
links.reason: Peirce used the pragmatic maxim against Kant's 'thing in itself' and judged Kant's logic shallow.

links.label: Descartes' first-person turn
links.reason: Husserl credited Descartes with the decisive first-person turn (his Cartesian Meditations), while rejecting most Cartesian doctrines.

sources.section: 3. The transcendental turn: Epoché, phenomenological reduction, and transcendental idealism

links.label: idealism it broke from
links.reason: Moore and Russell broke away from absolute idealism, and Hegel became a main target of the founders of analytic philosophy.

links.label: Quine's pragmatist themes
links.reason: C. I. Lewis and Quine developed pragmatist themes inside the analytic tradition.

links.label: empiricism rebuilt with logic
links.reason: Logical positivists (Vienna Circle): the Vienna Circle set out to reconceive empiricism using modern logic and science.

links.label: synthetic a priori banned
links.reason: Logical positivists (Vienna Circle): the Circle banned Kant's synthetic a priori as refuted by the progress of science.

sources.section: 3.2 The Analytic/Synthetic Distinction and the Relative A Priori

links.label: the Schoolmen's a priori
links.reason: Logical positivists (Vienna Circle): the analytic/synthetic distinction was used as a weapon against the 'substantive a priori of the Schoolmen' as well as Kant.

sources.section: 3.2 The Analytic/Synthetic Distinction and the Relative A Priori

links.label: its starting point
links.reason: The Frankfurt School revised and updated Marxism, taking Marx as the model of radical critique.

links.label: Hegel's method of critique
links.reason: Hegel has been a continual reference point, his method used as a model of immanent critique.

links.label: reason turned domination
links.reason: Horkheimer and Adorno's Dialectic of Enlightenment traces how Enlightenment reason became instrumental and an instrument of domination.

links.label: Habermas's critique
links.reason: Habermas argued that postmodernism contradicts itself and sought to rehabilitate modern reason against it.

links.label: the decentred subject
links.reason: Existentialism's critique of foundations and grand narratives, and Nietzsche and Heidegger in particular, shaped Derrida and Foucault.

links.label: Husserl deconstructed
links.reason: Derrida's Voice and Phenomenon criticises Husserl's founding 'principle of all principles'; Foucault rejected Sartre's privileging of the subject.

sources.section: 3. Basic Argumentation and its Implications: Time, Hearing-Oneself-Speak, the Secret, and Sovereignty

links.label: Marx read structurally
links.reason: The poststructuralists worked with structuralist readings of Marx; Foucault took up Marx through Althusser.

links.label: Beauvoir's Second Sex
links.reason: Beauvoir, a major existentialist, wrote The Second Sex (1949), the groundbreaking work feminist philosophers turn back to.

links.label: analytic feminism
links.reason: Feminist philosophy emerged from all major traditions; analytic feminism is one of its main approaches.

links.label: pragmatist feminism
links.reason: Pragmatist feminism is one of the approaches SEP lists.

links.label: feminist critical theory
links.reason: Third-generation critical theorists such as Fraser and Benhabib tried to make critical theory more amenable to feminism.

links.label: Butler's gender theory
links.reason: Feminist critical theory has a poststructuralist strand (Judith Butler), and analytic feminists also draw on Foucault and Butler.
